nameStory: The 'great' in great blue lobelia refers to its impressive height and robust stature compared to other lobelias in the region. It's also called blue cardinal flower because its brilliant blue spikes rival the stunning red display of its famous cousin, the cardinal flower, creating a perfect patriotic pair in late summer wetlands.
description: Great blue lobelia is a striking wildflower that sends up tall spikes of brilliant blue flowers from late summer into fall. This herbaceous perennial grows 2-4 feet tall with sturdy, unbranched stems lined with lance-shaped leaves. The tubular blue flowers cluster densely along the upper portion of the stem, creating an eye-catching display that's hard to miss in wetland areas. Though it's a perennial, individual plants are short-lived, typically lasting only a few years.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant blue tubular flowers arranged in a dense spike along the upper stem. Each flower has an unusual split-lip design with three lower petals fused together forming a landing pad, and two upper petals that arch backward. The flowers feel slightly waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately up the stem, getting smaller toward the top. The leaves feel smooth and slightly thick, with finely toothed edges that you can feel by running your finger along the margin.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single, sturdy, unbranched stems rising 2-4 feet tall from the base. The plant has a robust, upright appearance with the flower spike occupying the top third of the stem.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small brown capsules develop after flowering, splitting open to release tiny seeds. The dried seed capsules persist into winter, creating a rattling sound when shaken.

habitat: Great blue lobelia thrives in consistently moist to wet soils along stream banks, pond edges, wet meadows, and marshes throughout New England. It prefers partial shade to full sun and rich, organic soils that stay damp year-round. You'll often find it growing alongside cardinal flower, swamp milkweed, and various sedges in these wetland communities.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of lance-shaped leaves close to the ground. Plants are easily overlooked at this stage as they focus energy on root development.
seasonality.summer: Tall flower spikes begin developing in mid to late summer, with the brilliant blue flowers opening from bottom to top on the spike from August onward.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming continues through September and into October, making this one of the latest-blooming native wildflowers. Seeds ripen in brown capsules as flowers fade.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely, leaving dried brown seed stalks that may persist. Look for the rattling seed capsules and remember the wet locations for next year's display.

funFact: Great blue lobelia has evolved a clever weight-sensing mechanism - only bees heavy enough to depress the flower's lower petal landing pad can trigger the pollination process, causing the flower's stigma to lower and brush pollen onto the bee's back like a tiny botanical tollbooth!
confusionNotes: The brilliant blue color makes this plant quite distinctive, but it's sometimes confused with wild lupine, which has similar blue flower spikes. Remember that lupine has palm-shaped compound leaves and grows in dry, sandy soils, while great blue lobelia has simple lance-shaped leaves and always grows in wet areas.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its species name 'siphilitica,' this plant was never actually an effective treatment for syphilis, though it was mistakenly used for this purpose by early settlers. The name reflects historical medical practices rather than any real medicinal value.
compareHints: Among New England's lobelias, great blue lobelia is easily distinguished by its brilliant blue color and robust size. Cardinal flower is similar in structure but bright red, while Indian tobacco is much smaller with tiny pale blue or white flowers. The other regional lobelias are all considerably smaller and less showy than this impressive wetland species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cardinal flower stands out dramatically from its lobelia relatives—while great blue lobelia produces similar tubular flowers in blue, and Indian tobacco has tiny pale flowers, only cardinal flower blazes in brilliant red.
Unlike its showier relatives cardinal flower (bright red) and great blue lobelia (deep blue), Indian tobacco has much smaller, paler flowers.
Unlike its showy red cousin cardinal flower or the tall blue spikes of great blue lobelia, water lobelia is the only member of the lobelia family that lives completely underwater.
Among New England's lobelias, pale-spiked lobelia is the wallflower of the family with its subtle white or pale blue flowers.
Kalm's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its showy relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue, much larger).
Garden lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its New England native relatives like cardinal flower and great blue lobelia, which are tall, upright wetland plants.

Unlike its native Lobelia relatives such as cardinal flower or great blue lobelia which grow as upright leafy stems with showy flower spikes, matted pratia is a tiny mat-forming groundcover with individual star-shaped flowers.
Nuttall's lobelia is much smaller and more delicate than its famous relatives like cardinal flower (bright red) or great blue lobelia (deep blue and tall).
